definition.text: A sustainability-linked bond is a bond whose terms, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets.

facts.text: Performance is tracked with key performance indicators measured against sustainability performance targets.
Unlike green, social or sustainability bonds, the money raised can be used for general purposes.
Italian utility Enel issued the first in September 2019, promising a 25 basis point penalty on its coupon if it missed its target.
Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020; over 85% were tied to environmental indicators, most often emissions cuts.

title: Trophy hunting

definition.text: Trophy hunting is hunting for sport in which parts of the killed animal, such as the head, horns or hide, are kept and displayed.

facts.text: Supporters argue it gives economic reasons to conserve wildlife areas: 'if it pays it stays'.
The IUCN recognises that well-managed trophy hunting can create strong incentives to conserve species and habitats outside protected areas.
After South Africa legalised white rhino hunting, landowners reintroduced the species and numbers rose from under one hundred to more than 11,000.
Poorly managed, it can distort age and sex structures, disrupt social groups and cause population declines.
A 2017 Economists at Large report found trophy hunting was under one percent of tourism revenue in eight African countries, and critics say little reaches local communities.

contested_note: Supporters say trophy hunting funds conservation, while opponents say it is immoral and brings little money to conservation or local people.

definition.text: A bond is a loan in the form of a tradable security: the issuer borrows money and promises to pay the holder interest and repay the principal.

facts.text: Interest is usually paid at fixed intervals, often every six months or every year.
Bonds fund borrowers' long-term investments, or for governments, current spending.
Bondholders are lenders while stockholders are owners; bondholders are repaid first if the company goes bankrupt.
Bonds usually have a fixed term, or maturity, unlike stocks; most last less than 30 years.
They are issued by governments, banks, companies and international institutions, and are mostly bought by institutions such as pension funds and insurers.
The coupon is the interest rate the issuer pays; it can be fixed or float with a reference rate.

definition.text: A bond's yield is the rate of return an investor earns from it.

facts.text: Current yield is the yearly interest divided by the bond's market price.
Yield to maturity estimates the total return from buying at today's price and holding to the end, counting the present value of all payments.
Yield and price move in opposite directions: when market interest rates rise, bond prices fall.

definition.text: Credit quality is how likely a bond's borrower is to pay the promised amounts on time rather than default.

facts.text: High-yield bonds are rated below investment grade by credit rating agencies.
Because they are riskier, investors expect a higher yield from them.

definition.text: Bonds are grouped by issuer, currency, term and the conditions attached to them.

facts.text: Government or treasury bonds are issued by national governments; the safest, risk-free bonds pay the lowest interest.
Bonds under five years are often called short, 5 to 15 years medium, and over 15 years long.
Fixed-rate bonds pay a constant coupon, while floating rate notes pay a coupon linked to a reference rate.
Convertible bonds can be swapped for the issuer's shares, mixing debt and equity.
